title: Exploring modulation of TRIP effects on localized corrosion behavior of medium-manganese steel
abstract: This study explores modulation of TRIP effects on localized corrosion behavior of medium-manganese steel, through a combination of computational simulations and multi-scale characterization methods. Results demonstrate Mn doping enhances stiffness and toughness in both BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe phases while reducing surface energy, thereby lowering corrosion susceptibility. Pre-straining triggers the TRIP effects through phase transformation of metastable retained austenite to deformation-induced martensite, which enhances yield strength and hardness while increasing dislocation density and stress concentration. Hence, micro-galvanic cells are formed between deformation-induced martensite and ferrite/retained austenite phases, which promotes pitting corrosion. Additionally, pre-straining elevates corrosion current density while decreasing polarization resistance, confirming the degradation of corrosion resistance. While the TRIP effects enhance mechanical performance, it increases localized corrosion risks due to microstructural heterogeneity, stress concentration and corrosion product film instability. These findings emphasize the need to balance mechanical properties and corrosion resistance in medium-manganese steels for marine engineering applications.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Medium-manganese steels (MMS), characterized by their manganese content ranging between 3% and 12%, have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their remarkable combination of strength, ductility, and toughness [ 1 , 2 ]. These steels are particularly promising for lightweight automotive applications, such as A-pillars, B-pillars, door beams, and bumper reinforcements, where high specific strength and excellent crash energy absorption are critical [ 3 , 4 ]. The distinctive mechanical properties of MMS can be primarily ascribed to the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, which improves strain hardening behavior by facilitating the dynamic phase transformation of retained austenite (RA) into martensite under mechanical stress [ 5–8 ]. In some MMS compositions, the discontinuous nature of TRIP effect can give rise to the Portevin–Le Chatelier (PLC) effect manifested as serrations in the stress–strain curve, which reflects dynamic strain aging and intermittent phase transformation [ 9 ]. This phenomenon not only improves the steel's mechanical performance but also makes it a potential candidate for applications in sectors demanding superior strength and formability, such as automotive and structural engineering [ 10–12 ]. Despite their promising mechanical attributes, MMS face challenges related to their localized corrosion susceptibility in marine environments, which can compromise their long-term durability and limit their practical applications [ 13 ]. Therefore, understanding the underlying mechanism of how TRIP effect influences localized corrosion is crucial for optimizing the performance of MMS.

TRIP effect in MMS is driven by the metastable RA, whose dynamic transformation into martensite under mechanical loading provides exceptional strain hardening and mechanical stability [ 14 ]. The formation and stability of this RA are critically governed by the alloying design and thermomechanical processing. Manganese (Mn) is the key austenite stabilizer that suppresses the ferrite-to-austenite transformation temperature and enables the retention of austenite at room temperature. Carbon (C) further enhances austenite stability by partitioning into the austenite phase during intercritical annealing (IA), while simultaneously strengthening the matrix through solid solution and carbide formation. Aluminum (Al) and silicon (Si) are commonly added to suppress cementite precipitation during annealing, thereby promoting carbon enrichment in austenite and improving its stability. Al also reduces surface oxidation during processing [ 15 , 16 ]. A pivotal microstructural feature in MMS is the formation of reversed austenite during IA—a process in which austenite nucleates and grows from the martensitic or ferritic matrix upon heating into the ( α  +  γ ) two-phase region [ 17 ]. This reversed austenite, enriched in Mn and C due to partitioning during annealing, constitutes the primary source of RA after final quenching. Its volume fraction, morphology, and chemical stability directly dictate the magnitude of TRIP effect and, consequently, the balance between strength and ductility [ 3 ]. For instance, Jia et al. [ 18 ] demonstrated that increasing Mn content enhances austenite stability, improving ductility while maintaining high strength. Similarly, Zou et al. [ 19 ] emphasized that TRIP effect is strongly dependent on the volume fraction and stability of RA, which can be optimized through careful adjustments in Mn content and heat treatment processes. These studies underscore the critical role of Mn and the TRIP effect in achieving an optimal balance between strength and ductility in MMS. Furthermore, understanding the microstructural factors that influence corrosion resistance, as well as how TRIP effect governs localized corrosion processes, is also essential to fully exploit the potential of MMS.

Recent studies suggest that TRIP effect, while beneficial for mechanical performance, may also affect corrosion behavior by altering the local electrochemical environment through phase transformation [ 20–23 ]. For instance, Papula et al. [ 24 ] investigated hydrogen-induced delayed cracking susceptibility in TRIP-aided ferritic-austenitic low-alloy steels, demonstrating that strain-induced martensitic transformation reduces the crack-arresting tendency of RA, while the presence of  α ′-martensite increases hydrogen embrittlement sensitivity. However, while these studies provide valuable insights into the macroscopic trends, the intrinsic mechanisms governing microscale corrosion influenced by TRIP effect remain unclear. Specifically, the application of advanced computational simulations and multi-scale characterization techniques to probe the localized corrosion mechanism associated with TRIP-induced phase transformations has been relatively limited. Key questions remain regarding how strain-induced phase transformation impacts local electrochemical heterogeneity and corrosion susceptibility. This knowledge gap poses a significant challenge to the optimization of MMS for applications demanding both superior mechanical performance and excellent corrosion resistance.

The application of first-principles calculations has emerged as a powerful tool for elucidating the fundamental mechanisms governing the mechanical and electrochemical behavior of MMS [ 25–30 ]. By simulating the electronic structure, density of states, and adsorption energies of elements like Mn, such computational approaches provide insights into phase stability, surface chemistry, and mechanical properties at the atomic scale. Moreover, first-principles calculations enable the exploration of the effects of Mn doping on the lattice constants, work functions, and surface energies of different phases in MMS. These methods are particularly useful in understanding the electronic interactions between RA and martensite, which may influence localized corrosion susceptibility. These theoretical predictions, when combined with experimental techniques such as nanoindentation, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and electrochemical tests, facilitate a deeper understanding of the microstructural evolution, mechanical performance, and corrosion behavior of MMS.

This study investigates the influence of TRIP effect on the localized corrosion susceptibility of MMS through a combination of first-principles calculations and experimental techniques. Techniques such as focused ion beam - transmission electron microscopy (FIB-TEM) and transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD) are instrumental in visualizing the phase transformation and defect interactions at the nanoscale. Furthermore, methods like the scanning vibrating electrode technique (SVET) are employed to evaluate the localized electrochemical corrosion behavior of MMS in seawater environments. The integration of these experimental methods with theoretical modeling bridges the gap between microstructural features, mechanical performance, and corrosion initiation and propagation mechanisms. This research aims to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the influence of localized corrosion behavior by TRIP effect, providing insights for the development of MMS with enhanced mechanical and corrosion-resistant properties.

sections.heading: First-principles calculations
paragraphs:
First-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) to investigate the effects of Mn on the mechanical properties and corrosion susceptibility of high-strength steel. The calculations included evaluations of elastic modulus, work function, surface energy, density of states (DOS), and Cl adsorption energy. The elastic constant matrix was determined via the strain-stress method, with post-processing conducted using VASPKIT. The projector-augmented wave (PAW) method described ion-electron interactions, and the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional was employed. Computational parameters comprised an 11 × 11 × 11 k-point mesh, a plane-wave cutoff energy of 600 eV, and convergence criteria of 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ eV for energy and 0.015 eV/Å for forces. Energy-lattice parameter relationships for body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) Fe phases were fitted using the Birch-Murnaghan (BM) equation of state ( Eqs. (1)  and ( 2 )) [ 31 ], yielding equilibrium lattice constants of 0.283 nm (BCC) and 0.345 nm (FCC) ( Fig. 1 
                         ), in close agreement with both experimental data and previous DFT results [ 32–34 ].

sections.heading: Material preparation
paragraphs:
Experimental steel (mass fraction, %: C 0.36, Si 0.015, Mn 8.12, Al 1.86, Fe balance) underwent heat treatment involving austenitization at 950°C, air cooling, holding at 700°C for 1 h, water quenching, tempering at 400°C for 1 h, and air cooling, resulting in a dual-phase microstructure. Time-temperature-transformation (TTT) curves plotted using JMatPro ( Fig. 4 
                         (a)) indicated Ac1 and Ac3 temperatures of 656.4 and 774.9°C, respectively. FactSage software with FSstel, FactPS, and FToxide databases was employed to calculate equilibrium phase diagrams as a function of temperature ( Fig. 4 (b)), which guided the selection of the IA temperature (700°C) to ensure a two-phase ( α  +  γ ) region. The heat treatment process is shown in  Fig. 4 (c). Austenitization at 950°C and IA at 700°C were performed using a box-type furnace (model FURNACE-1300), while tempering at 400°C was conducted in a salt bath furnace (model XH/D).

sections.heading: FIB-TEM
paragraphs:
Focused ion beam (FIB) technology was used to prepare thin lamellae (<80 nm) from pre-strained steel samples containing ferrite, martensite, austenite, and deformation-induced martensite for transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis, using a Thermo Scientific Scios 2 FIB/SEM system. The target region was identified under scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and a protective Pt layer was deposited to prevent Ga +  ion damage. The area was cut using FIB, and the lamella was transferred to a lift-out grid via a micromanipulator needle and attached with Pt deposition ( Fig. 5 
                         ). Final thinning (30 kV to 5 kV, 0.5 nA to 50 pA) minimized damage. An FEI Tecnai F30 TEM equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) was used to analyze elemental distribution and crystal structures.

sections.heading: Nanoindentation tests
paragraphs: This study employed a Nano Indenter G200X to measure the mechanical properties of the micro-regions in the steel samples. During the tests, the experimental conditions were set with a maximum applied load of 20 mN, and the spacing between each indentation point was 12 μm. After completing the nanoindentation tests, the indented regions were characterized using EBSD to distinguish the variations in the micromechanical properties among different microstructures. The EBSD data were analyzed using AZtecCrystal software to evaluate grain size, misorientation, and conduct phase reconstruction along with proportion analysis [ 35 ]. The obtained depth-load curves and hardness values were then analyzed in detail.

sections.heading: Slow strain rate tension tests
paragraphs:
Pre-straining was performed on a slow strain rate tensile testing machine (model YYF-50) at 0.1 mm/min under a load of 1 σ 
                         s . After pre-straining, the applied load was fully removed, and the samples were unloaded and stored at ambient conditions prior to subsequent testing. Tensile tests on both the original and pre-strained steel were conducted to determine yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation, with two parallel specimens tested for each condition. The reported values are averages with standard deviations (±12 MPa for yield strength, ±18 MPa for tensile strength, and ±1.0% for elongation). A contact extensometer (gauge length: 25 mm) was attached to the gauge section during testing to directly measure strain and eliminate errors caused by machine compliance (e.g., grip slippage or frame deformation). The yield strength was defined as the 0.2% offset proof stress based on the extensometer-recorded strain. Post-fracture surfaces were analyzed to study the microstructure. All tests were conducted in accordance with the GB/T 15970.1–2018 standard, using strip-shaped specimens (180 mm × 25 mm × 2 mm) with a 32 mm × 10 mm gauge section and  φ 8 mm holes at both ends. The tensile testing strain rate was set at 0.0096 mm/min.

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: Specimens (10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm) were polished with silicon carbide sandpapers (up to 1500 grit) and diamond paste (W2.5) to achieve a mirror finish, then ultrasonically cleaned with ethanol and air-dried. After etching in 4 vol.% nitric acid-ethanol solution, the microstructures of residual austenite, ferrite, martensite, and deformation-induced martensite were characterized using SEM (Apreo S HiVac, Oxford Instruments). To study initial corrosion, the etched samples were immersed in 0.5 wt.% NaCl solution for 5–10 min, dried with alcohol, and observed under SEM to analyze corrosion in specific regions.

Crystal structure, grain size, local misorientation distribution (kernel average misorientation, KAM), and phase fraction were further analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) on the same SEM system. EBSD mapping was conducted with a step size of 0.08 μm, an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, and a magnification of 5000 × . EBSD data were processed using Channel 5 software (Oxford Instruments).

X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using an X’pert PRO MPD diffractometer with Cu  K α 
                          radiation (Cu target) to determine phase fractions and retained austenite content. The diffraction patterns were collected over a 2 θ  range of 40°–100°.

Microstructural distribution and phase transformations were analyzed using TEM (JEM-F200, JEOL) operated at 200 kV. Diffraction patterns were processed in DM software for orientation calibration, and phase identification was completed using Jade software (Materials Data, Inc.). For TEM sample preparation, specimens were mechanically thinned to 70 μm, followed by electrolytic twin-jet polishing at -20°C under 70 V in a solution of 4 vol.% perchloric acid and 96 vol.% ethanol.

sections.heading: Electrochemical tests
paragraphs: Micro-zone electrochemical test was conducted using a SVET system (VersaScan, AMETEK, Advanced Measurement Technology) to analyze the local corrosion current density of medium-Mn steel in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. A vibrating Pt-Ir probe (∼5 μm diameter, 80 Hz) was used to detect ionic concentration gradients, converting potential signals into current density using the equation  I  = -Δ E / R  (where the solution resistance  R  = 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ Ω). The probe's vibration (30 μm amplitude) enabled precise mapping of corrosion behavior over varied immersion durations, providing detailed insights into surface redox reactions and the local current distribution.

Electrochemical tests were carried out using a Zahner Zennium electrochemical workstation equipped with a conventional three-electrode system. The test sample functioned as the working electrode, a platinum mesh was utilized as the counter electrode, and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) acted as the reference electrode. Potentiodynamic polarization curves were recorded at a scan rate of 0.5 mV/s within a potential range of ±300 mV relative to the open-circuit potential. To ensure data reliability and accuracy, all electrochemical tests were conducted in triplicate.

sections.heading: First-principles calculations
paragraphs: To investigate the influence of Mn doping on the mechanical properties and corrosion susceptibility of BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe, first-principles calculations were performed. Density of states (DOS), work function, surface energy, adsorption energy, and mechanical parameters were analyzed for pure Fe and Mn-doped Fe with BCC and FCC structures.

Fig. 6 
                         (a) compares the bulk modulus, Young's modulus, and shear modulus for pure and Mn-doped BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe. Mn doping slightly improves the mechanical properties of BCC-Fe (e.g., shear modulus increases from 83.3 GPa to 86.0 GPa) and marginally decreases those of FCC-Fe (e.g., Young's modulus decreases from 414.9 GPa to 406.0 GPa).  Fig. 6 (b) shows that Mn doping slightly alters Poisson's ratio and increases elastic anisotropy for both structures, with FCC-Fe-Mn exhibiting the highest anisotropy.  Fig. 6 (c) compares Pugh's ratio ( B / G ) and Vickers hardness for pure and Mn-doped BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe. For BCC-Fe, Mn doping increases hardness (from 8.1 GPa to 8.6 GPa), while FCC-Fe exhibits a slight hardness reduction (from 19.6 GPa to 18.5 GPa), reflecting a trade-off between ductility and strength.

Fig. 7 
                         (a) and (b) shows DOS of Mn-doped and undoped BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe, respectively. In both structures, Mn doping introduces resonant states near the Fermi level, indicating strong hybridization between Mn and Fe orbitals. This suggests enhanced covalent bonding and electronic interaction, which may contribute to the modified mechanical properties discussed earlier.  Fig. 7 (c) reveals that Mn doping has only a marginal effect on the work function (e.g., BCC-Fe: 4.481 eV; BCC-Fe-Mn: 4.495 eV). However, Mn doping significantly reduces surface energy for both structures, as seen in  Fig. 7 (c). For example, the surface energy decreases from 5.829 J/m² to 5.589 J/m² in BCC-Fe and from 3.397 J/m² to 3.257 J/m² in FCC-Fe, indicating improved surface stability. These findings demonstrate that while preserving the bulk electronic structure, Mn doping enhances surface cohesion, thereby improving surface stability.

Fig. 8 
                          illustrates the adsorption energy and equilibrium adsorption distance of Cl atoms on BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe before and after Mn doping. The corrosion tendency of the Fe matrix in a marine environment can be analyzed based on the adsorption energy and equilibrium adsorption distance of Cl atoms [ 36–40 ]. A more negative adsorption energy indicates that Cl atoms are more likely to adsorb on the surface, thereby promoting corrosion. As shown in  Fig. 8 (a), in both BCC and FCC structures, the absolute values of adsorption energy at all adsorption sites increase after Mn doping, indicating that Cl adsorption on the Fe surface becomes more stable, which theoretically may enhance the corrosion tendency. On the other hand, the equilibrium adsorption distance reflects the average distance between Cl atoms and the Fe matrix. A shorter distance suggests more stable adsorption, facilitating Cl accumulation on the surface and promoting corrosion, whereas a longer distance indicates that Cl is less likely to adsorb, which helps reduce corrosion susceptibility. As shown in  Fig. 8 (b), the equilibrium adsorption distance at all adsorption sites increases in both BCC and FCC structures after Mn doping, suggesting that Cl atoms find it more difficult to approach the Fe surface, thereby reducing Cl adsorption stability and lowering corrosion susceptibility. This indicates that Mn doping helps mitigate the corrosion tendency of both Fe-based structures against Cl attack.

Comprehensive analysis shows that the effect of Mn doping on Cl-induced corrosion exhibits a competitive relationship, where the increase in equilibrium adsorption distance partially offsets the corrosion tendency caused by the enhanced adsorption energy. Therefore, Mn doping helps mitigate the corrosion effect of Cl on both BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe structures. Overall, Mn doping reduces surface energy and improves corrosion resistance for both BCC-Fe and FCC-Fe, while slightly enhancing mechanical properties for BCC-Fe.

sections.heading: Microstructure characterization before corrosion
paragraphs: Microstructures of the original and pre-strained steel samples were characterized using XRD, SEM, EBSD, TEM, and FIB-TKD to analyze phase distribution, stress concentration, dislocation density, and Mn distribution, as well as to study TRIP effect.

Phase composition of the steel sample before and after deformation was analyzed using XRD, and the corresponding results are shown in  Fig. 9 
                         . The diffraction patterns exhibited typical characteristic peaks of FCC austenite on (111), (200), and (220) crystal planes, as well as diffraction peaks of BCC phases (bainite and martensite) on (110), (200), and (211) crystal planes. With increasing pre-strain load, the intensity of the (111)  γ -austenite characteristic peak decreased, and the (200)  γ -austenite peak gradually disappeared, indicating that the pre-strain significantly affected the austenite content in the steel and reduced the diffraction peak intensity of the austenite phase.

The volume fraction of austenite and the carbon content in the steel before and after pre-straining were quantitatively analyzed by XRD, and the corresponding results are presented in  Table 1 
                         . It can be seen that the RA content in the steel changed significantly with the change in the pre-straining load. The RA and carbon contents in the original steel were 23.1% and 1.4%, respectively. When the pre-straining load was increased from 0 to 1 σ 
                         s , the RA content decreased from 23.1% to 20.9%, and the carbon content increased from 1.4% to 1.6%. It happened because metastable RA with a low carbon content in the original steel underwent martensitic transformation under the action of the pre-strain, leaving the stable RA with a high carbon content.

As shown in  Fig. 10 
                         , EBSD maps of the original and pre-strained samples (red: BCC phase, blue: FCC phase) indicate a reduction in the austenite phase after pre-straining. This transformation correlates with TRIP effect, where metastable austenite transforms into deformation-induced martensite under applied strain. The inverse pole figure (IPF) maps, now accompanied by a standard color key correlating hue to crystallographic direction (<001> in blue, <101> in green, and <111> in purple), reveal that the original steel exhibits a predominant <101> orientation with a minor <001> component. After pre-straining, the texture shifts toward <111> and <001> orientations, suggesting significant lattice rotation and plastic deformation induced by pre-straining. This evolution of crystallographic texture aligns with recent studies on intercritically annealed medium-Mn steels, where strain-induced phase transformation and dislocation activity drive orientation redistribution in both BCC and FCC phases [ 4 , 9 , 16 , 23 ].

KAM maps ( Fig. 10 (d) and (h)) are complemented by corresponding KAM distribution histograms ( Fig. 10 (d1) and (d2) for the original sample;  Fig. 10 (h1) and (h2) for the pre-strained sample), which quantify the misorientation gradient within BCC and FCC phases. Notably, these histograms show no substantial shift in peak position or full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) between the original and pre-strained conditions, indicating that the overall statistical distribution of local lattice distortions remains largely unchanged. This suggests that while pre-straining induces phase transformation and macroscopic plasticity, the average dislocation density and associated lattice curvature at the micron-scale resolution of EBSD do not increase significantly, implying that plastic deformation is accommodated primarily through dislocation glide rather than accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) at this scale. The lack of pronounced KAM elevation also hints that severe localized strain gradients may be confined to sub-micron regions, necessitating higher-resolution techniques like TEM-Geometric Phase Analysis (GPA) for precise mapping.

Meanwhile, KAM maps show no significant visual changes before and after pre-straining, consistent with the statistical analysis. Further characterization using TEM combined with GPA is required to precisely evaluate nanoscale strain distribution.

Samples were extracted from the pre-strained steel using FIB-SEM. FIB-TKD images of the pre-strained steel, along with SEM images before and after pre-straining, are shown in  Fig. 11 
                         . TKD mapping of the pre-strained steel, combined with SEM microstructural characterization before and after pre-straining, reveals the microstructural features and phase transformation behavior of the steel in both its original and pre-strained states. The TKD map on the left displays the phase distribution of FCC (red) and BCC (green), where RA is present in a discontinuous form. Additionally, during the pre-straining process, the metastable austenite undergoes partial but incomplete transformation into strain-induced martensite (M′). This is attributed to the heterogeneous distribution of strain and the varying stability of austenite grains. Under applied deformation, regions of austenite with lower mechanical stability preferentially transform into martensite, while more stable austenite regions retain their FCC structure. The incomplete transformation suggests that the pre-straining conditions did not provide sufficient driving force to fully destabilize all metastable austenite, leaving residual austenite embedded within the martensitic matrix.

SEM characterization further illustrates the effect of pre-straining on the microstructure. In the original steel, RA is distributed in a lath or block-like form between ferrite (F) and martensite (M). However, in the pre-strained steel, due to strain-induced phase transformation, a portion of the RA transforms into blocky strain-induced martensite (M′). Microstructure of the pre-strained sample exhibits a significant presence of blocky martensite (M′), indicating that pre-straining promotes the phase transformation of metastable austenite into martensite.

Combined TKD and SEM results demonstrate that pre-straining induces localized phase transformation. TKD analysis directly reveals the conversion of RA to martensite, while SEM imaging documents the associated microstructural evolution, particularly the formation of blocky strain-induced martensite. These findings highlight how mechanical strain governs austenite destabilization and subsequent microstructural modifications.

To further investigate the morphology and distribution of the microstructure and dislocations in the samples, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) was used to characterize the strain conditions at the interfaces before and after pre-straining. Additionally, inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) images and GPA maps of the phase interfaces before and after pre-straining were compared.

Fig. 12 
                          presents the HRTEM images of the phase interfaces in the samples before and after pre-straining, along with the corresponding GPA strain maps. GPA calculates the microscopic strain using specialized software, where the local strain magnitude can be interpreted by comparing the color distribution with the reference scale [ 41 ].  Fig. 12 (a) shows the macroscopic morphology of the original steel, while  Fig. 12 (b) presents a high-magnification HAADF image of the same sample. In this image, the light gray regions correspond to RA, and the dark gray regions represent ferrite. In  Fig. 12 (b), the red dashed box marks the phase interface position in the original steel sample. By comparing the GPA maps before and after pre-straining, it is evident that before pre-straining, the strain distribution at the phase interface is relatively uniform, as shown in  Fig. 12 (b4). This observation confirmed the higher dislocation density at the phase interface observed in the IFFT image, as shown in  Fig. 12 (b3). In the studied steel, the elevated stacking fault energy due to Mn and Al alloying suppresses  ε -martensite formation, promoting direct  γ  (FCC) →  α ′ (BCC/BCT) transformation during deformation. Thus, TRIP effect occurs primarily through direct austenite-to- α ′-martensite transformation without an intermediate HCP phase.

However, further comparative analysis of the HRTEM and GPA images of the phase interface under pre-straining conditions reveals significant changes in the pre-strained sample ( Fig. 12 (c)). Macroscopic morphology shows a noticeable transformation; originally continuous lath-shaped RA becomes fragmented after pre-straining. Moreover, in  Fig. 12 (d), the deformation-induced martensite region displays higher strain levels, with localized strain concentrations at the phase interface. This indicates a substantial accumulation of dislocations within the pre-strained steel, primarily concentrated in the deformation-induced martensite, as illustrated in  Fig. 12 (d4). This finding is consistent with the IFFT analysis, which also reveals a high dislocation density at the phase interface, as shown in  Fig. 12 (d3).

SAED and fast Fourier transform (FFT) analyses were performed across the RA/ferrite and RA/martensite interfaces to examine crystallographic orientation relationships. As shown in the inset of  Fig. 12 (f), the diffraction spots from the RA ( γ ) and adjacent lath martensite ( α ′) satisfy the Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) orientation relationship: (011) α ′ // (111) γ  (as shown in  Fig. 12 (e, f)). This K-S relationship is consistent with recent findings in medium-Mn steels processed by IA, where reversed austenite forms in close crystallographic registry with the parent lath martensite matrix [ 42 ]. The presence of this orientation relationship facilitates coherent or semi-coherent interfaces, which can influence both mechanical response and local electrochemical behavior.

In summary, pre-straining induces TRIP effect, leading to a reduction in austenite and the formation of blocky deformation-induced martensite with increased stress concentration and dislocation density.

sections.heading: Macro- and micro-mechanical properties
paragraphs: Macro- and micro-mechanical properties of the original and pre-strained steel samples were evaluated using slow strain rate tensile tests (SSRT) and nanoindentation testing, respectively. The observed changes in mechanical properties are closely linked to TRIP effect, which significantly influences phase transformation and stress distribution.

Fig. 13 
                          and  Table 2 
                          summarize SSRT results of the original and pre-strained samples. Pre-straining increased the yield strength (YS) from 841.5 MPa to 996.7 MPa, which can be attributed to TRIP effect. During pre-straining, metastable austenite ( γ ) transforms into deformation-induced martensite (M′), increasing the dislocation density and enhancing the strength of the material. The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) remains largely unchanged, while the total elongation (TEL) decreases slightly. This reduction in ductility is due to the depletion of metastable austenite, which reduces the capacity for further phase transformation under load. Similarly, the plastic strain energy (PSE) decreased from 18.2% to 16.5%, as TRIP effect diminishes after most of the austenite has already transformed into martensite during pre-straining. The work-hardening rate curves further confirm that the original sample exhibits a sustained high hardening rate at intermediate strains, which is characteristic of active TRIP. In contrast, the pre-strained sample shows an earlier drop in the work-hardening rate, consistent with the exhaustion of RA.

Nanoindentation testing was conducted to provide localized insights into mechanical properties across different phases. In the tested steel sample, the nanoindentation tests were conducted in a 4 × 4 matrix arrangement, with 16 indentation points measured to obtain the depth-load curves, as shown in  Figs. 14 and 15 
                         
                         . Based on the curve characteristics, the indentation points were classified into hard regions and soft regions. Under a fixed maximum load testing mode, the hard regions corresponded to smaller indentation depths, whereas the soft regions exhibited greater depths.

By correlating with EBSD images, it was found that the hard regions primarily corresponded to RA and deformation-induced martensite (M′), while the soft regions corresponded to ferrite (F) and deformation-induced martensite (M). Typical points A1 and A2 were selected from the hard regions, and B1 and B2 from the soft regions, to analyze their depth-load curves and mechanical property data ( Table 3 
                         ).

In the tested steel, the hardness and elastic modulus of the hard regions (A1 and A2) are significantly higher than those of the soft regions (B1 and B2). Specifically, the hardness of A1 and A2 was 3.9 and 4.2 GPa, respectively, with elastic moduli of 176.4 and 202.5 GPa. This performance enhancement is mainly attributed to the stress-induced martensitic transformation of metastable RA during indentation, which generates harder deformation-induced martensite, thereby significantly improving the local mechanical properties. In contrast, the hardness values of B1 and B2 in the soft regions were 3.7 and 3.0 GPa, with elastic moduli of 188.3 and 162.7 GPa, respectively. The soft regions mainly consisted of ferrite and deformation-induced martensite, and since no significant phase transformation occurred, they exhibit lower hardness and elastic modulus.

From the depth-load curves, it can be observed that the curves of the hard regions (A1, A2) are steeper, reflecting higher hardness and strength, while those of the soft regions (B1, B2) are relatively gentler, indicating lower hardness. In the hard regions, the transformation of RA into deformation-induced martensite during indentation significantly enhanced local hardness, forming a "hardening effect", whereas the soft regions mainly exhibited the intrinsic properties of the base microstructure.

TRIP effect plays a crucial role in the observed mechanical behavior. During deformation, the transformation of metastable austenite into martensite contributes to strain hardening, improving strength while maintaining ductility. However, after pre-straining, much of the metastable austenite has already transformed into deformation-induced martensite, leaving less austenite available for further transformation during deformation. This weakens TRIP effect and reduces ductility. At the micro-scale, regions with M'/RA demonstrate enhanced hardness and modulus due to the localized transformation of austenite into martensite and the associated increase in dislocation density. In contrast, M/F regions lack this transformation, resulting in relatively lower mechanical performance. Overall, pre-straining enhances macro-scale strength through TRIP effect but slightly reduces ductility due to the depletion of metastable austenite, while micro-scale TRIP effect contributes to the superior hardness and stiffness of M'/RA regions, emphasizing the critical role of phase transformation in mechanical property evolution.

sections.heading: Initial corrosion characterization
paragraphs:
Initial corrosion behavior of the original and pre-strained steel samples was studied using SKPFM and SEM. SKPFM characterization of the original sample ( Fig. 16 
                         ) revealed a potential difference between phases, particularly between metastable austenite ( γ ) and ferrite ( α ). Metastable austenite typically exhibits a higher Volta potential than ferrite and martensite, rendering it cathodic relative to BCC phases. Consequently, ferrite and strain-induced martensite act as anodes in the micro-galvanic couples, while austenite serves as the cathode. This electrochemical configuration drives preferential anodic dissolution of the ferrite/martensite regions adjacent to austenite, making phase boundaries susceptible sites for localized corrosion initiation [ 43 ].

First-principles calculations in  Section 3.1  further confirm that the work function of FCC-structured doped systems is consistently higher than that of BCC-structured doped systems, indicating that the corrosion tendency of the FCC-structured iron matrix is always lower than that of the BCC-structured iron matrix. This difference leads to the formation of a micro-galvanic effect. Due to their higher electrochemical activity, martensite and metastable austenite are more susceptible to corrosion, which may facilitate localized corrosion initiation under corrosive conditions.

SEM analysis of the initial corrosion features in both samples ( Fig. 17 
                         ) revealed significant differences. The original sample showed a time-dependent corrosion behavior. After 5 min of immersion, slight pitting appears on the surface. As immersion time increases to 10 min, the surface changes from slight pitting to relatively uniform corrosion. Statistical analysis shows that the average pit diameter increases from approximately 0.7 µm at 5 min to approximately 1.2 µm at 10 min, confirming that pits grow in size with prolonged exposure. This trend is also visually evident across multiple fields of view, where 10-minute pits are consistently larger and more developed than those at 5 min. This behavior can be attributed to the even distribution of metastable austenite and ferrite phases in the absence of pre-straining. Additionally, the original sample exhibits relatively low stress concentration and dislocation density, which minimizes localized corrosion activity. SKPFM characterization confirms that the homogeneous microstructure, which prevents the formation of micro-galvanic cells, allows corrosion to proceed evenly over the surface.

In contrast, the pre-strained sample exhibited accelerated localized corrosion in the form of pitting, shown in  Fig. 17 . After 5 min of immersion, more pronounced pitting appeared on surface, forming small pit-like defects. As immersion time extends to 10 min, these pits grow in size and expand further, yet the corrosion remains localized in the form of pitting rather than transitioning to uniform corrosion. This change in corrosion behavior is closely linked to TRIP effect. During pre-straining, metastable austenite transforms into deformation-induced martensite (M′), creating a microstructure with higher phase heterogeneity. The newly formed martensite contains significant stress concentrations and a higher dislocation density, as observed in prior microstructure characterization. These features act as active anodic sites, promoting localized corrosion. Furthermore, the potential difference between ferrite and deformation-induced martensite becomes more pronounced due to the strain energy stored in the martensite, intensifying the micro-galvanic effect and driving localized corrosion.

The differences in corrosion behavior between the original and pre-strained samples are primarily due to microstructural changes induced by TRIP effect. In the pre-strained sample, the transformation of metastable austenite into martensite increases the susceptibility to localized corrosion by creating stress concentrations and dislocation-rich regions. This, combined with the intensified electrochemical activity at phase boundaries, not only accelerates uniform corrosion but also exacerbates pitting corrosion in the pre-strained sample.

sections.heading: Macro- and micro-electrochemical tests
paragraphs: The macro- and micro-electrochemical behavior of the original and pre-strained steel samples was analyzed using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), potentiodynamic polarization (PDP), and SVET. Results reveal that pre-straining significantly affects both the electrochemical kinetics and localized corrosion behavior, driven by microstructural changes associated with TRIP effect.

Electrochemical test results are shown in  Fig. 18 
                         , with fitting data presented in  Table 4 
                         . Potentiodynamic polarization curves ( Fig. 18 (a)) indicate that corrosion current density ( i 
                         corr ) of the pre-strained sample (1.2 × 10⁻⁵ A cm -2 ) is higher than that of original sample (6.9 × 10⁻⁶ A cm -2 ). It reflects a higher corrosion rate in the pre-strained steel. This behavior can be attributed to TRIP effect, which increases the phase heterogeneity and stress concentration in the pre-strained steel, making it electrochemically more active.

Impedance spectra ( Fig. 18 (b–d)) and their fitted parameters further highlight the differences in corrosion resistance between the two samples. The solution resistance ( R 
                         s ) and film resistance ( R 
                         f ) of the pre-strained sample are slightly lower than those of the original sample, indicating a thinner or less protective surface film. Similarly, the charge transfer resistance ( R 
                         ct ) and polarization resistance ( R 
                         p ) of the pre-strained sample (1011 and 1083.9 Ω cm², respectively) are lower than those of the original sample (1082 and 1165.5 Ω cm², respectively), confirming the reduced overall corrosion resistance. Additionally, the double-layer capacitance (C dl ) of the pre-strained sample (3.7 × 10⁻⁴ F) is higher than that of the original sample (2.4 × 10⁻⁴ F), which reflects an increased active surface area due to localized corrosion, consistent with the microstructural effects of martensite transformation.

The observed differences in macro- and micro-electrochemical behavior can be attributed to TRIP effect. In the pre-strained sample, the transformation of metastable austenite into deformation-induced martensite introduces phase heterogeneity, stress concentrations, and increased dislocation density. These microstructural changes enhance localized electrochemical activity and reduce the stability of the corrosion product film, making the pre-strained steel more susceptible to pitting corrosion. In contrast, the original sample, with its more uniform microstructure and lower stress levels, exhibits better corrosion resistance, as evidenced by its lower corrosion current density, higher polarization resistance, and more uniform current distribution. In summary, more uniform microstructure and lower stress levels in the original sample result in superior corrosion resistance with a tendency toward relatively uniform corrosion rather than localized attack.

sections.heading: Effects of Mn addition on corrosion susceptibility and TRIP effects
paragraphs: First-principles calculations reveal a critical trade-off between mechanical properties and corrosion resistance in Mn-doped MMS. While Mn doping enhances the stiffness and hardness of BCC-Fe, it slightly reduces the mechanical performance of FCC-Fe, indicating phase-dependent strengthening effects. However, Mn doping consistently lowers surface energy and increases the equilibrium adsorption distance of Cl⁻, mitigating corrosion susceptibility in both BCC and FCC structures. This suggests that Mn incorporation improves corrosion resistance by stabilizing the surface against aggressive chloride ions, despite its complex influence on bulk mechanical properties [ 44–47 ].

The distribution of Mn across different phases further modulates corrosion behavior by altering the local electrochemical properties and phase stability. As observed in FIB-TEM and EDS/TKD analyses ( Fig. 21 
                         ), Mn preferentially segregates in RA, stabilizing the FCC phase and delaying its transformation during deformation through its strong austenite-stabilizing effect. This Mn enrichment in RA not only enhances austenite stability but also significantly influences the electrochemical heterogeneity between phases by creating composition gradients. The higher work function of FCC-Fe compared to BCC-Fe, as confirmed by first-principles calculations, establishes a pronounced micro-galvanic effect between RA and ferrite/martensite, promoting localized corrosion at phase boundaries where the potential difference is maximized.

The addition of Mn significantly alters the stability of austenite by promoting its chemical stabilization and delaying its transformation under mechanical deformation. This stabilization effect, however, is only partial in metastable austenite, allowing it to gradually transform into body-centered structures such as martensite when subjected to strain. During this transformation process, the evolving microstructure introduces substantial heterogeneity, including newly formed interfaces, dislocation networks, and localized stress concentrations. These features act as preferential sites for electrochemical activity. While Mn also contributes to improved corrosion resistance by lowering surface energy and inhibiting Cl⁻ adsorption, the strain-induced phase transformation counters this benefit by generating micro-galvanic coupling between the transformed and untransformed regions, thereby promoting localized corrosion through defect-assisted dissolution mechanisms.

sections.heading: Modulation of TRIP effects on mechanical properties
paragraphs: The TRIP effects in MMS are governed by the strain-induced transformation of metastable austenite into martensite, which exhibits distinct morphological and kinetic characteristics [ 48–50 ]. EBSD and TEM analyses reveal that blocky and lath-like RA grains exhibit varying transformation tendencies under strain, with blocky RA showing incomplete transformation due to higher mechanical stability. This inhomogeneous phase evolution leads to a mixed microstructure of untransformed RA, deformation-induced martensite (M′), and ferrite, contributing to heterogeneous strain distribution. Mn segregation in RA further stabilizes the FCC phase, delaying transformation and refining the martensitic structure, which enhances strain hardening.

In MMS, the morphology of RA plays a crucial role in governing its transformation behavior under applied strain. EBSD and TEM analyses reveal that RA exists primarily in blocky and lath-like forms, each exhibiting distinct mechanical stability and transformation tendencies. Blocky RA, due to its larger size and lower interface density, demonstrates higher mechanical stability and is more resistant to transformation during deformation. In contrast, lath-like RA, with its finer and more fragmented structure, transforms more readily into martensite under similar strain conditions. This morphological dependence leads to an inhomogeneous phase evolution during deformation, resulting in a complex microstructure composed of partially transformed RA, deformation-induced martensite (M′), and ferrite. Such heterogeneity contributes to uneven strain distribution and localized stress concentrations. Additionally, Mn segregation preferentially stabilizes the FCC structure in RA, further delaying transformation and refining the emerging martensitic morphology, ultimately enhancing strain hardening behavior.

The mechanical responses observed in the present Fe-8.12Mn-1.86Al-0.36C steel characterized by high strength and sustained ductility are comparable to recent medium-Mn systems with tailored compositions. For instance, Wan et al. [ 51 ] reported an MMS achieving 841 MPa UTS with 16.4% elongation after intercritical annealing, while a flash annealing MMS exhibited 1312 MPa strength and 15.4% ductility with pronounced TRIP activity. The slightly higher carbon content in our alloy enhances austenite stability and promotes a more continuous TRIP response, resulting in a similarly favorable strength–ductility balance without sacrificing work hardening capacity.

The formation of this multiphase structure triggers complex mechanical responses [ 52–54 ]. During deformation, dynamic phase transformation not only elevates dislocation density but, more critically, establishes a unique stress partitioning mechanism between soft and hard phases. Nanoindentation and GPA strain mapping demonstrate this mechanism. M′/RA regions exhibit pronounced dislocation accumulation and localized strain hardening, displaying markedly higher hardness and elastic modulus than ferrite regions. Importantly, this microstructural heterogeneity is not static but continuously evolves during deformation, progressively enhancing material strength through work hardening while maintaining ductility via plastic deformation of untransformed phases.

Overall, the continuous transformation of RA into martensite during deformation contributes to progressive strain hardening, thereby improving the material's strength and ability to withstand higher stresses. Additionally, the heterogeneous microstructure, characterized by the coexistence of ferrite, RA, and M′, ensures effective stress partitioning, which enhances fracture resistance.

sections.heading: Modulation of TRIP effect on local corrosion behaviour
paragraphs:
TRIP effect plays a crucial role in affecting localized corrosion behavior by altering phase distribution, electrochemical heterogeneity, and stress accumulation. Electrochemical analysis and SKPFM results in  Section 3.4  reveal that pre-straining transforms metastable austenite into deformation-induced martensite, increasing microstructural heterogeneity and promoting localized corrosion. The schematic diagrams of corrosion mechanism of original steel and pre-strained steel in a seawater environment are demonstrated in  Fig. 22 
                         . The original steel exhibits a relatively uniform corrosion trend ( Fig. 22 (a) and (c)), whereas the pre-strained steel shows distinct pitting corrosion features ( Fig. 22 (b) and (d)). This difference is attributed to the TRIP-induced phase transformation, which enhances micro-galvanic activity and stress concentration at phase boundaries.

The corrosion mechanism of the original steel ( Fig. 22 (a) and (c)) is dominated by uniform corrosion due to its relatively homogeneous microstructure and lower stress levels. RA and ferrite form a stable electrochemical environment, minimizing localized corrosion initiation. In contrast, the pre-strained steel ( Fig. 22 (b) and (d)) exhibits localized corrosion due to the formation of micro-galvanic cells between deformation-induced martensite and ferrite or RA. SKPFM potential mapping confirms that deformation-induced martensite has a lower electrochemical potential than surrounding phases, acting as an anodic site for localized corrosion initiation. Stress distribution and dislocation density further influence localized corrosion behavior. HRTEM and GPA strain mapping in  Section 3.2  indicate that pre-straining increases strain accumulation at phase interfaces, particularly between austenite and martensite. These stress concentrations act as preferential sites for corrosion initiation, accelerating localized attack. Additionally, the higher dislocation density in deformation-induced martensite enhances anodic dissolution, further promoting pitting corrosion of pre-strained steel.

Comparative analysis of EIS and SVET results in  Section 3.5  confirms that the pre-strained steel exhibits higher corrosion current density and lower polarization resistance than the original steel. The formation of localized anodic sites in deformation-induced martensite accelerates pitting corrosion, while the instability of the corrosion product film in pre-strained regions further exacerbates localized attack.

In summary, TRIP effect significantly influences localized corrosion behavior by altering the microstructure and electrochemical environment [ 55 , 56 ]. The transformation of RA into deformation-induced martensite increases phase heterogeneity, leading to electrochemical potential differences that promote micro-galvanic corrosion [ 57–60 ]. The newly formed martensite regions, characterized by high dislocation density and localized stress concentration, become anodic sites prone to accelerated dissolution and corrosion product film instability. As a result, the corrosion mechanism shifts from relatively uniform corrosion in the original steel to pronounced pitting corrosion in the pre-strained state. This TRIP-corrosion coupling behavior aligns with recent findings in Al-containing medium-Mn steels. For example, Mohapatra et al. [ 43 ] observed that increased phase heterogeneity due to strain-induced martensite in Fe-7Mn-4Al-0.18C steel similarly elevated localized corrosion susceptibility, despite excellent mechanical properties. While TRIP effect enhances strength and hardness, it simultaneously raises the risk of localized corrosion. Therefore, optimizing alloy composition and heat treatment processes to control phase distribution and minimize residual stress is essential for achieving a balance between mechanical performance and corrosion resistance in MMS.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This study investigated the modulation of pre-straining, Mn doping, and the TRIP effect on the mechanical properties and corrosion behavior of steel. Through a combination of first-principles calculation, microstructural characterization, mechanical testing, and electrochemical analysis, the following conclusions were drawn: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Mn doping enhances the mechanical properties of MMS by increasing hardness and stiffness in BCC-Fe and improving toughness in FCC-Fe. Additionally, it lowers the surface energy and increases the Cl⁻ adsorption distance in both BCC and FCC phases, indicating an alleviation in corrosion susceptibility. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Pre-straining induces TRIP effect, transforming metastable austenite into martensite, increasing phase heterogeneity and dislocation density, which enhances yield strength but slightly reduces ductility and elongation. At the microscale, this phase transformation significantly improves the hardness and stiffness of M'/RA regions. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The original sample exhibits relatively uniform corrosion, while the pre-strained sample demonstrates mainly pitting corrosion. Martensitic transformation not only increases micro-galvanic cells and promotes anodic dissolution in martensite regions, but also introduces significant stress concentration and dislocation accumulation at phase interfaces. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            Electrochemical tests reveal that pre-straining increases the corrosion current density and decreases polarization resistance, indicating reduced overall corrosion resistance and increased susceptibility to localized corrosion. 
                         
                         
                            (5) 
                            TRIP effect enhances steel strength but simultaneously increases localized corrosion risk due to phase heterogeneity, stress concentration and corrosion product film instability. The results provide fundamental insights for designing advanced high-strength steels with balanced mechanical properties and corrosion resistance for marine engineering applications.
